chief_complaint: sudden hives, lip swelling, and throat tightness after eating a peanut cookie
hpi_details: 29M presents with sudden eruption of itchy hives (urticaria) all over his body, swelling of his lips and tongue, and a feeling of throat tightness. Symptoms began 15 minutes after eating a cookie that may have contained peanuts.
ideas: knows he is having a severe allergic reaction to peanuts
concerns: terrified of airway closure and suffocation

core_concepts: Anaphylaxis is a severe, rapidly progressive IgE-mediated systemic hypersensitivity reaction involving two or more organ systems (skin/mucosa, respiratory, cardiovascular, GI) after allergen exposure.
Peanut is one of the most common and potent food triggers; reactions in a previously sensitized patient can begin within minutes of ingestion.
Intramuscular epinephrine in the anterolateral thigh is the first-line, life-saving treatment and should never be delayed for antihistamines or steroids.
Biphasic reactions can occur hours after apparent resolution, so patients need a period of observation and clear return-precautions instructions.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden hives, lip swelling, and throat tightness after eating a peanut cookie

Key HPI features: 29M presents with sudden eruption of itchy hives (urticaria) all over his body, swelling of his lips and tongue, and a feeling of throat tightness. Symptoms began 15 minutes after eating a cookie that may have contained peanuts.
Objective/Exam findings: Diffuse urticaria, lip/tongue angioedema, and possible stridor or wheeze, with tachycardia or hypotension in more severe reactions.
Relevant background/PMH: Peanut allergy diagnosed in childhood
Current medications: EpiPen (expired 2 years ago, not carried)
common_misconceptions: Waiting to see if the hives 'settle down' before giving epinephrine, rather than treating airway and systemic symptoms immediately.
Giving an antihistamine alone and considering the reaction treated, when epinephrine is the definitive first-line therapy.
Assuming a patient who improved after one epinephrine dose no longer needs observation for a possible biphasic reaction.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to localized oral allergy syndrome (no systemic involvement) without completing a comprehensive assessment.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Throat tightness or difficulty swallowing.
management_principles: Administer intramuscular epinephrine 0.3mg immediately in the anterolateral thigh; repeat every 5-15 minutes if symptoms persist.
Assess and support airway, breathing, and circulation; give IV fluids for hypotension.
Observe in the ED for a period based on reaction severity and biphasic-reaction risk.
Prescribe two epinephrine auto-injectors and refer to Allergy for confirmation testing and an anaphylaxis action plan.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: World Allergy Organization (WAO) Anaphylaxis & Angioedema Guidelines

reference_soap.subjective: 29M presents with sudden eruption of itchy hives (urticaria) all over his body, swelling of his lips and tongue, and a feeling of throat tightness. Symptoms began 15 minutes after eating a cookie that may have contained peanuts.
reference_soap.objective: Diffuse urticaria, lip/tongue angioedema, mild inspiratory stridor. Vitals show tachycardia; blood pressure currently stable.
reference_soap.assessment: Anaphylaxis, likely peanut-triggered, in a patient with known peanut allergy and no current epinephrine auto-injector.
reference_soap.plan: Administer intramuscular Epinephrine 0.3mg immediately in the anterolateral thigh and assess airway, breathing, and circulation. Give IV fluids for hypotension or shock. Antihistamines may be used only as adjuncts for skin symptoms after epinephrine; corticosteroids are not routine acute treatment. Observe in the ED for a duration based on reaction severity and biphasic-reaction risk. Refer to Allergy, prescribe current epinephrine auto-injectors, and provide comprehensive patient counseling.

learning_objectives: Recognize the clinical features and diagnostic criteria of anaphylaxis.
Formulate a prioritized differential diagnosis for sudden hives, lip swelling, and throat tightness after eating a peanut cookie
Select the correct first-line emergency treatment and appropriate observation period for anaphylaxis
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies for peanut-triggered anaphylaxis.

teaching.one_liner: A severe, rapid-onset IgE-mediated systemic reaction to peanut protein with skin, oral, and airway involvement — treat with intramuscular epinephrine first.
differentials: Localized oral allergy syndrome (no systemic involvement)
red_flags: Known prior anaphylaxis to the same food

must_ask.objective: What was eaten and onset timing
must_ask.say: What did you eat, and how soon after did the symptoms start?
Does your throat feel tight, or is it hard to breathe?
Do you have hives, or swelling of your lips or tongue?
Have you been diagnosed with a peanut allergy before?
Do you carry an epinephrine auto-injector, and have you used it?

history.answer: I ate a cookie about fifteen minutes ago that might have had peanuts in it, and now I'm covered in itchy hives, my lips are blowing up, and my throat feels tight.
The hives broke out all over my chest and arms about fifteen minutes after eating that cookie, and then spread across my whole body within minutes.
It is everywhere right now, covering my neck, chest, stomach, back, and both of my arms and legs.
They look like raised, puffy red welts and blotches all over my skin.
It itches intensely like crazy all over, but my skin does not feel painful or burning.
No, they all showed up at the same time right after the cookie and have stayed flared up.
I had a bad reaction like this when I was seven years old after accidentally eating peanut butter candy, and they gave me a shot in the ER.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or muscle aches.
My lips and tongue are swollen, but there are no sores, peeling, or blisters inside my mouth, eyes, or anywhere else.
No, my skin isn't peeling or falling off, and there are no dark purple spots.
Yes, my lips and tongue started swelling right away, and my throat feels like it is constricting and closing up.
I am having a hard time getting air in, and I feel a little lightheaded and shaky.
I took a bite of a homemade cookie someone brought to campus, and right after swallowing I realized it tasted like peanut butter.
No, I haven't started any new prescription drugs, antibiotics, or painkillers.
No, I haven't used any new soaps, colognes, lotions, or jewelry, and I haven't touched any unusual plants.
No one around me has anything like this; it started right after I ate that peanut cookie.
No, I haven't been bitten by any insects, and I haven't been hiking or traveling recently.
No, I didn't put any creams or ointments on because everything happened so fast and I ran straight here.
I am sexually active with one partner, and neither of us has any genital sores, ulcers, or discharge.
No, my joints don't hurt at all, and my nails look completely normal.
I have allergic rhinitis in the spring, but I've never had asthma or eczema.
I have an EpiPen prescription from years ago, but it expired two years ago and I left it sitting in my desk at home.
I know this is a severe allergic reaction to peanuts because it feels just like when I was a kid.
I'm terrified my throat is going to clamp shut completely and I won't be able to breathe.
I need an epinephrine injection right away to open up my throat before it closes.
Just a severe peanut allergy diagnosed in childhood; otherwise I have been healthy.
I haven't had any surgeries, and my only hospitalization was for that peanut reaction when I was seven.
I don't take any regular medications, and like I said, my EpiPen is expired at home.
I don't have any known drug allergies that I know of.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used vape products.
I only have a beer or two occasionally on weekends, none today.
I'm a graduate student and I live in an apartment off campus with a roommate.
My mother has seasonal allergies and asthma, but no one else has severe food allergies.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, heart rate 118 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8°C.
Anxious, flushed young man in mild respiratory distress with audible high-pitched breathing.
Diffuse erythematous, raised wheals with pale centers over the neck, chest, abdomen, and limbs that blanch with pressure; no skin peeling or bullae.
Pronounced swelling of both lips and anterior tongue with mild uvular edema; no oral ulcers or bleeding.
Mild inspiratory stridor heard loudest over the trachea and scattered high-pitched expiratory wheezes throughout both lung fields.
Tachycardic rate with regular rhythm; normal heart sounds with no murmurs or rubs.
Mild bilateral eyelid swelling; conjunctivae are clear without injection or ulcerations.
No palpable cervical or submandibular lymphadenopathy.
Soft and non-tender throughout with normal bowel sounds; no masses or organomegaly.
